title: Zenos’s Allegory Introduced
summary: Jacob recalls the words of Zenos, who likens the house of Israel to a tame olive tree nourished in a vineyard until it grows old and begins to decay.

explicit_facts.text: Jacob refers to Zenos’s words to the house of Israel.
Zenos calls the house of Israel to hear his words as a prophet of the Lord.
The Lord likens the house of Israel to a tame olive tree that a man nourishes in a vineyard; it grows old and begins to decay.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The olive tree and vineyard can be shown as illustrations of the allegory being related.
unspecified_visual_details: Whether Jacob is visibly present while the allegory is recounted.
The identities and appearances of Zenos and the man in the allegory.

narration.text: Behold, my brethren, do ye not remember to have read the words of the prophet Zenos,
I will liken thee, O house of Israel, like unto a tame olive-tree

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The olive tree is explicitly a likeness for the house of Israel, not a separate literal event.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict the allegory as a literal historical event involving named historical people.

title: The Tree Is Pruned
summary: The master sees the tame olive tree beginning to decay, says he will care for it, and prunes, digs around, and nourishes it.

explicit_facts.text: The master sees the olive tree beginning to decay and says he will prune, dig around, and nourish it so it may produce young branches and not perish.
The master prunes, digs around, and nourishes the tree as he said.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The master tends the tree with pruning and digging implements.
unspecified_visual_details: The master’s appearance, clothing, and tools.

narration.text: I will prune it, and dig about it, and nourish it

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The action is part of the olive-tree allegory.
prohibited_inventions: Do not show the tree already producing branches in this moment.

title: Young Branches, Dying Top
summary: The tree puts forth a few young, tender branches, but its main top begins to perish. The master tells his servant to bring wild olive branches and says the withering main branches will be burned.

explicit_facts.text: After many days, the tree puts forth a few young, tender branches while its main top begins to perish.
The master tells the servant to bring branches from a wild olive tree and says the withering main branches will be cast into the fire.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The tree can show a few fresh shoots alongside a withering main top.
unspecified_visual_details: The appearance of the servant and the wild olive tree.

narration.text: It grieveth me that I should lose this tree

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The burning is commanded for the allegory’s branches; avoid graphic imagery.
prohibited_inventions: Do not show the branches being burned yet.

title: Branches Assigned and Grafted
summary: The Lord of the vineyard says he will graft young branches where he chooses and directs the servant to replace removed branches with wild olive branches. The servant does so.

explicit_facts.text: The Lord of the vineyard says he will take young, tender branches and graft them wherever he chooses, preserving their fruit.
He directs the servant to graft wild olive branches in place of the removed branches and to burn the removed branches.
The servant grafts in branches of the wild olive tree.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The servant can be shown grafting branches onto the tame olive tree.
unspecified_visual_details: The particular grafting technique and the appearance of the branches.

narration.text: Take thou the branches of the wild olive-tree, and graft them in, in the stead thereof

doctrinal_or_story_notes: Grafting is an explicit action within the allegory.
prohibited_inventions: Do not identify the branches with specific peoples or add an interpretation not stated in the supplied verses.

title: The Grafted Tree Is Nourished
summary: The Lord has the tree dug around, pruned, and nourished, then tells the servant to watch and care for it. He says he will place the natural branches in the lowest part of the vineyard to preserve them and their fruit.

explicit_facts.text: The Lord has the tree dug around, pruned, and nourished, hoping to preserve its roots.
The Lord tells the servant to watch and nourish the tree.
The Lord says he will place the natural branches in the nethermost part of the vineyard to preserve them and their fruit.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The Lord and servant can be shown beside the cared-for tree.
unspecified_visual_details: Where in the vineyard the Lord’s instruction is spoken.

narration.text: watch the tree, and nourish it, according to my words

doctrinal_or_story_notes: This remains an allegory; the natural branches are not specified as people physically present.
prohibited_inventions: Do not show the natural branches being moved before the next event.

title: Natural Branches Hidden
summary: The Lord goes and hides the tame olive tree’s natural branches in different parts of the lowest area of the vineyard.
locations: the nethermost part of the vineyard

explicit_facts.text: The Lord hides the natural branches in different parts of the nethermost vineyard according to his will.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The Lord places natural branches at more than one location in the vineyard.
unspecified_visual_details: The exact number and locations of the branches.
doctrinal_or_story_notes: The verse describes the branches being hidden, not people.
prohibited_inventions: Do not add the servant to this action; the verse names only the Lord as going and hiding the branches.

title: Return to the Grafted Tree
summary: After a long time, the Lord and servant return to labor in the vineyard. The servant points out the tree with grafted wild branches, which has sprung up and begun to bear good fruit like the natural fruit.

explicit_facts.text: After a long time, the Lord asks the servant to go down into the vineyard to labor.
The Lord and servant go down into the vineyard, and the servant draws attention to the tree.
The grafted tree has sprung forth and begun to bear good fruit like the natural fruit.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The tree can be shown bearing visible fruit.
unspecified_visual_details: The length of time passed and the tree’s precise appearance.

narration.text: Behold, look here; behold the tree.

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The scene occurs after a long time has passed; do not merge it with the earlier grafting.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict the tree’s harvest or storage of fruit yet.

title: Fruit Laid Up
summary: The Lord explains that the roots’ strength enabled the wild branches to produce tame fruit. He and the servant then visit the hidden natural branches; the first has borne much good fruit, which the Lord directs the servant to store.
locations: the nethermost part of the vineyard

explicit_facts.text: The Lord says the wild branches took moisture from the root, and its strength enabled them to produce tame fruit; he plans to store the fruit.
The Lord and servant go to the nethermost part to see whether the natural branches have borne fruit.
The first natural branch has borne much good fruit, and the Lord directs that its fruit be gathered and stored.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The first natural branch can be shown bearing abundant fruit, with the servant gathering some.
unspecified_visual_details: The exact appearance of the stored fruit and storage place.

narration.text: Take of the fruit thereof, and lay it up against the season

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The spoken explanation in verse 18 reports the allegory’s meaning of the roots and branches; do not visualize it as a separate supernatural event.
prohibited_inventions: Do not add a harvest from other branches at this moment.

title: Fruit in Poor Ground
summary: The servant asks why the Lord planted the fruitful tree in the vineyard’s poorest spot. The Lord answers that he knew the ground was poor and had nourished it for a long time.
locations: the nethermost part of the vineyard

explicit_facts.text: The servant asks why the tree was planted in the poorest spot in the vineyard.
The Lord says he knew the spot was poor and had nourished the tree for a long time; it has borne much fruit.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The tree and visibly poor ground can be shown together.
unspecified_visual_details: The visual features that make the soil the poorest spot.

narration.text: it was the poorest spot in all the land of thy vineyard

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The dialogue concerns the allegory’s tree and ground.
prohibited_inventions: Do not add a reason for planting there beyond what the Lord states.

title: More Branches Examined
summary: The Lord shows the servant another fruitful tree in ground poorer than the first, then another fruitful branch, and the last tree, planted in good ground, which bears both tame and wild fruit. He orders the bad branches removed and burned; the servant asks to nourish the tree longer.

explicit_facts.text: Another branch planted in poorer ground has borne much fruit, and the Lord directs that it be gathered and stored.
A further planted branch has been nourished and has borne fruit.
The last tree is in good ground; part bears tame fruit and part wild fruit, despite being nourished like the others.
The Lord orders branches that have not borne good fruit to be removed and cast into the fire.
The servant asks to prune, dig around, and nourish the tree longer in hope it will bear good fruit.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Show the last tree with distinct portions bearing tame and wild fruit.
unspecified_visual_details: The exact placement of the several trees within the vineyard.

narration.text: Let us prune it, and dig about it, and nourish it a little longer

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The verses describe sequentially shown branches and trees; avoid suggesting they are one tree.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict the ordered burning or the subsequent tending yet.

title: All the Vineyard Nourished
summary: The Lord and servant nourish all the vineyard’s fruit. After a long time, they return because the end is drawing near and find all sorts of fruit on the tree whose natural branches were removed and wild branches grafted in.

explicit_facts.text: The Lord and servant nourish all the fruit of the vineyard.
After a long time, the Lord calls the servant to labor again, saying the time draws near and fruit must be stored.
They go to the tree with natural branches removed and wild branches grafted in and find all sorts of fruit cumbering it.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The tree can be shown bearing a variety of fruit.
unspecified_visual_details: The specific appearance of the different kinds of fruit.
doctrinal_or_story_notes: A long time separates the earlier nourishment from this visit.
prohibited_inventions: Do not combine this visit with the later tasting and judgment of the fruit.

title: The Fruit Is Bad
summary: The Lord tastes each kind of fruit and finds that none is good. Grieved at the tree’s failure despite their labor, he asks the servant what should be done to preserve good fruit.

explicit_facts.text: The Lord tastes each kind of fruit and recalls that much fruit had been stored earlier.
The tree now bears no good fruit, only bad fruit, and the Lord grieves at the prospect of losing it.
The Lord asks what should be done to the tree to preserve good fruit.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The Lord can be shown examining and tasting fruit from the tree.
unspecified_visual_details: The appearance and taste of the bad fruit.

narration.text: there is none of it which is good

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The fruit is part of the allegorical tree; do not imply a separate event.
prohibited_inventions: Do not show the tree being cut down at this point.

title: Roots Still Alive
summary: The servant says the roots remain alive and good because the wild branches nourished them. The Lord says the tree and roots are of no benefit while it bears evil fruit, but notes the roots’ strength and explains that the wild branches have overrun them, causing evil fruit and decay.

explicit_facts.text: The servant says the wild branches nourished the roots, which remain alive and good.
The Lord says the tree and roots profit him nothing while the tree bears evil fruit.
The Lord says the roots are good and have produced good fruit through their strength.
The wild branches have overrun the roots, producing much evil fruit; the tree begins to perish and will soon be ready for the fire unless something is done.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The tree can show wild branches overgrowing the trunk and roots, with bad fruit.
unspecified_visual_details: How the allegorical roots and branches should be visually distinguished.

narration.text: the wild branches have grown and have overrun the roots thereof

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The Lord’s explanation is allegorical speech, not a separate narrated supernatural scene.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict roots visibly moving or acting.

title: The Hidden Branches Are Corrupt
summary: The Lord and servant go to the lowest parts of the vineyard and find that the fruit of the first, second, and last natural branches has become corrupt. On the last, wild fruit has overtaken the part that bore good fruit, and that branch has withered and died.
locations: the nethermost parts of the vineyard

explicit_facts.text: The Lord proposes checking whether the natural branches in the nethermost vineyard have borne evil fruit.
They find that the fruit of the first, second, and last natural branches has become corrupt.
On the last tree, wild fruit has overcome the good-bearing part, and that branch has withered and died.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Show the last tree with a withered branch beside the wild fruit that overtook it.
unspecified_visual_details: The exact appearance of the corrupt fruit.
doctrinal_or_story_notes: The branches are part of the allegory, not additional people.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict the tree being destroyed.

title: The Lord Weeps
summary: The Lord weeps and asks what more he could have done. He recounts that the last tree was planted in choice ground after obstructing growth was cleared away; good fruit was overcome by wild fruit. Despite his care, the trees are corrupt, and he grieves as he wonders who corrupted the vineyard.

explicit_facts.text: The Lord weeps and asks what more he could have done for the vineyard.
He says all fruit but the previously noted fruit became corrupted, and that the trees now seem fit only to be cut down and burned.
He says the last tree was planted in choice ground after he cleared what cumbered the spot; good fruit was overcome because he did not remove the other branches.
Despite extensive care, all the trees have become corrupt and are of no worth; the Lord grieves at losing them and asks who corrupted the vineyard.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The Lord can be visibly weeping beside the corrupted tree.
unspecified_visual_details: The servant’s reaction.

narration.text: What could I have done more for my vineyard?
Who is it that has corrupted my vineyard?

doctrinal_or_story_notes: Verses 43–45 recount earlier planting and growth as the Lord speaks; do not stage them as a present-time flashback.
prohibited_inventions: Do not invent a person or group responsible for corrupting the vineyard.

title: The Servant Explains the Corruption
summary: The servant suggests that the branches grew too lofty and overcame the good roots. The Lord proposes cutting down the trees, but the servant asks that the vineyard be spared longer. The Lord agrees because he grieves to lose the trees.

explicit_facts.text: The servant suggests the branches overcame the good roots by growing faster and taking strength for themselves.
The Lord proposes hewing down the trees and asks what more he could have done.
The servant asks the Lord to spare the vineyard a little longer.
The Lord agrees to spare it longer because he grieves to lose the trees.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The Lord and servant can be shown before the vineyard trees as they confer.
unspecified_visual_details: Any tools for the proposed cutting down.

narration.text: Spare it a little longer.

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The proposed destruction is not carried out in this scene.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict trees being cut down or burned.

title: A Plan to Graft Again
summary: The Lord proposes grafting branches from the trees in the lowest vineyard back into their mother tree, replacing the most bitter branches with natural branches. He says this may preserve the roots, and he will also graft branches among the scattered natural trees to preserve their roots and perhaps produce good fruit.

explicit_facts.text: The Lord proposes grafting branches from the trees in the nethermost vineyard into their source tree and replacing the most bitter branches with natural branches.
The Lord says this may preserve the tree’s roots for his purpose.
The Lord says the natural branches’ roots remain alive and proposes grafting branches among them and their mother tree so they may become strong and bear good fruit.

reasonable_visual_inferences: A diagram-like arrangement of trees and proposed grafting may help convey the instruction.
unspecified_visual_details: Whether the Lord gestures toward particular trees while explaining.

narration.text: let us graft them into the tree from whence they came

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The verses present a proposed plan, not yet its execution.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict the grafting as already completed.

title: Branches Grafted Between Trees
summary: The Lord and servant graft branches from the wild natural tree into the natural trees, and natural branches from those trees into their mother tree. The Lord directs them to remove only the most bitter wild branches, nourish and trim the trees, and remove branches ripened for destruction, hoping good will overcome evil.

explicit_facts.text: They graft branches from the natural tree that has become wild into the natural trees that have also become wild.
They graft branches from the natural trees into their mother tree.
The Lord orders that only the most bitter wild branches be removed and directs grafting as previously instructed.
The Lord says they will nourish and trim the trees and remove branches ripened to perish for burning.
The Lord hopes the roots will gain strength and good will overcome evil through the change of branches.
The Lord says he has preserved natural branches and roots and hopes the trees will again bear good fruit and bring him joy.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Show the Lord and servant grafting branches between trees and tending them.
unspecified_visual_details: The exact number and placement of trees and grafts.

narration.text: Pluck not the wild branches from the trees, save it be those which are most bitter

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The Lord’s future hopes in verses 59–60 are not depicted as already achieved.
prohibited_inventions: Do not show all wild branches removed; the instruction is to remove only the most bitter.

title: Servants Called to the Final Labor
summary: The Lord orders servants to be called for a final diligent labor, gives instructions for grafting and nourishing the trees, and says bad branches should be cleared gradually as good growth strengthens. The Lord sends his servant, who brings a few other servants.

explicit_facts.text: The Lord orders servants called to labor diligently so the natural fruit may return.
The Lord says this is the last time he will prune the vineyard and tells them to labor with their might.
He instructs them to graft branches and dig around old and young trees so all may be nourished.
He directs further tending and says to prepare for the last grafts if they grow and bear natural fruit.
He orders bitter branches cleared according to the strength and size of good growth, not all at once.
He directs them to clear away bad growth as good growth develops until good overcomes bad.
He says natural branches will be grafted again into the natural tree and into natural branches, bringing them together to bear natural fruit as one.
He says bad branches will be cast away from the vineyard and this will be its only pruning.
The Lord sends the servant, who does as commanded and brings a few other servants.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The Lord can be shown giving instructions, followed by the servant arriving with a few other servants.
unspecified_visual_details: The servants’ identities, appearances, and exact number.

narration.text: And the branches of the natural tree will I graft in again into the natural tree;

doctrinal_or_story_notes: Verses 61–69 are instructions and plans; the actual work begins in the following scene.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict a large or specifically numbered group of servants.

title: The Final Labor Begins
summary: The Lord tells the servants to labor with their might, saying this is the last time he will nourish the vineyard. The servants and the Lord labor together and obey his commandments.

explicit_facts.text: The Lord tells the servants to labor with their might and says this is the last time he will nourish the vineyard.
The servants and the Lord labor with their might and obey the Lord’s commandments in all things.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The Lord and servants can be shown tending trees together.
unspecified_visual_details: The specific tasks underway in this moment.

narration.text: Go to, and labor in the vineyard, with your might.

doctrinal_or_story_notes: This is the final labor declared in the allegory.
prohibited_inventions: Do not show the final harvest or end state before the next verses.

title: Natural Fruit Returns
summary: Natural fruit begins to return. Natural branches thrive as wild branches are removed, with root and top kept equal in strength. The labor continues until the bad is removed and the trees bear natural fruit as one body, with equal fruit.

explicit_facts.text: Natural fruit begins to appear again; natural branches thrive, wild branches are removed, and root and top are kept equal in strength.
The servants labor until the bad is removed and the trees again bear natural fruit, becoming like one body with equal fruits.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The trees can be shown bearing natural fruit while servants continue tending them.
unspecified_visual_details: The precise appearance of natural versus wild fruit.
doctrinal_or_story_notes: The verse compares the trees to one body; do not depict them literally merging into a single tree.
prohibited_inventions: Do not add a visible supernatural transformation of the trees.

title: The Vineyard Is No More Corrupt
summary: Seeing good fruit and a vineyard no longer corrupt, the Lord calls up the servants and praises their diligence and obedience. He says he has preserved the natural fruit and will store it for a long time.

explicit_facts.text: The Lord sees good fruit and a vineyard no longer corrupt, calls his servants, and says he has preserved the natural fruit.
The Lord blesses the servants for their diligence and says they will share joy with him because the vineyard is no longer corrupted.
The Lord says he will store the vineyard’s fruit for a long time, as promised.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The Lord can be shown addressing the gathered servants among the fruitful trees.
unspecified_visual_details: The servants’ appearance and the means of storing the fruit.

narration.text: Behold, for this last time have we nourished my vineyard

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The speech describes the completed labor and the Lord’s future storage of fruit.
prohibited_inventions: Do not show a later return of evil fruit in this scene.

title: The Vineyard’s End Foretold
summary: The Lord says that when evil fruit again comes into the vineyard, the good and bad will be gathered; he will preserve the good and cast away the bad, and afterward the vineyard will be burned.

explicit_facts.text: The Lord says that when evil fruit again comes, the good and bad will be gathered; the good will be preserved and the bad cast away.
The Lord says that afterward the season and end will come and the vineyard will be burned with fire.

reasonable_visual_inferences: A symbolic image of good and bad fruit separated may accompany the Lord’s stated future plan.
unspecified_visual_details: When this future event occurs and how the gathering and burning appear.

narration.text: then cometh the season and the end

doctrinal_or_story_notes: This is a future event described in the Lord’s speech, not a present-time event in the vineyard.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict the future gathering or burning as occurring now.
